guide.text: A front-wheel skid costs steering and balance at once. Release the lever immediately.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Stopping Quickly in a Curve.

content.question: You must stop quickly in a curve, but straightening up first would carry you off the road. How should you brake?

choices.text: Smoothly and gradually, adding pressure as you straighten
As hard as you can, right away, while still leaned over
With the rear brake only, so the front cannot lock
Not at all until you are through the curve

content.explanation: When you cannot straighten first, brake gently while leaned, then reduce your lean and add brake pressure as you slow, until the motorcycle is straight and you can brake fully.

guide.text: If you can't straighten up before braking in a curve, brake gently, then add pressure as you straighten.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Stopping Quickly in a Curve.

content.question: You are braking to a stop in a curve. What should you do with the handlebars in the last few feet?

choices.text: Straighten them, so you stay balanced and upright
Turn them slightly toward the curb
Keep them turned the way you were leaning
Let them go loose so the front wheel can settle

content.explanation: In the last few feet of the stop, square the handlebars so the motorcycle comes to rest straight up and balanced.

guide.text: When stopping in a curve, straighten the handlebars in the last few feet.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Rear-Wheel Skids.

content.question: Too much rear brake pressure locks the rear wheel. What do you lose the moment it locks?

choices.text: The ability to change direction
All of your braking
The use of your front brake
Grip on the front tire

content.explanation: As soon as the rear wheel locks, you can no longer change direction. A skidding rear tire can lead to a violent crash.

guide.text: Too much rear brake locks the rear wheel, and a locked rear wheel cannot change direction.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Swerving or Turning Quickly.

content.question: You need to swerve right around an obstacle, then carry on in your original direction. How do you use the handgrips?

choices.text: Press the right grip to swerve, then the left grip once you are clear
Press the left grip to swerve, then the right grip once you are clear
Press the right grip and hold it there until you have stopped
Turn the handlebars right, then let them center on their own

content.explanation: Press the handgrip on the side you want to go, right to go right, and the motorcycle leans quickly that way. Once you are clear, press the opposite grip to return to your original direction.

guide.text: To swerve, press the handgrip on the side you want to go, then press the opposite grip once you are clear.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Swerving or Turning Quickly.

content.question: You are swerving around an obstacle. What should your body do?

choices.text: Stay upright, knees on the tank, as the motorcycle leans under you
Lean with the motorcycle at the same angle, as in a normal turn
Lean the opposite way to keep the motorcycle as upright as possible
Rise off the seat so your knees can absorb the movement

content.explanation: Let the motorcycle lean toward your escape path while your body stays upright above it. Press your knees into the tank and keep your feet planted on the footrests.

guide.text: In a swerve, stay upright and let the motorcycle lean under you, knees pressed to the tank and feet planted.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Swerving or Turning Quickly.

content.question: As you swerve around an obstacle, where should you look?

choices.text: At your escape path
At the obstacle, so you can judge how far to clear it
Down at the road just ahead of your front tire
In your mirror, to see what is behind you

content.explanation: Make your escape path the target of your vision. Looking where you want to go helps you control your path of travel.

guide.text: In a swerve, make your escape path the target of your vision.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Swerving or Turning Quickly.

content.question: You have to swerve around an obstacle and slow down as well. When should you brake?

choices.text: Before or after the swerve, never during it
During the swerve, so you slow as you go around
During the swerve, but with the rear brake only
Not at all, since the swerve takes the place of braking

content.explanation: Separate braking from swerving: brake, then swerve, or swerve, then brake. Never brake while you are swerving.

guide.text: Separate braking from swerving: brake before or after, never during.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Curves.

content.question: What is a primary cause of single-vehicle motorcycle crashes, the ones where no other vehicle is involved?

choices.text: Running wide in a curve or turn
Braking too hard on a straight road
A tire failing at highway speed
Being pushed off line by a crosswind

content.explanation: A primary cause of single-vehicle crashes is riders running wide in a curve or turn. Ride every curve within your skill level and the posted speed limit.

guide.text: Running wide in a curve or turn is a primary cause of single-vehicle crashes.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Curves.

content.question: You are about to ride a curve you have never ridden before. What should you keep in mind?

choices.text: It may stay the same, widen, tighten or turn again
It will keep the same sharpness it shows at the entry
It will open up as you go, so you can speed up through it
Its sharpest point will be right at the entry

content.explanation: Every curve is different. Be alert to whether it stays constant, gradually widens, gets tighter or involves more turns, and ride within your skill level and the posted speed limit.

guide.text: Every curve is different: it may stay constant, widen, tighten or lead into more turns.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Curves.

content.question: How should you choose your path through a curve?

choices.text: Adjust your position for traffic, road conditions and the curve
Follow the curve of the road, since it is built as the safest line
Take whichever line lets you keep your speed up
Follow the line of the vehicle ahead of you

content.explanation: The road's own curve is not always the best line through it. Move within your lane to suit traffic, conditions on the road and the shape of the curve.

guide.text: The best line through a curve isn't always the road's own curve; set your lane position for traffic, conditions and the curve's shape.

meta.sourceSection: The Rider and the Motorcycle.

content.question: How does a motorcycle compare with a car in the way it handles?

choices.text: It responds faster, but rough roads and crosswinds affect it more
It responds faster, and its small size lets it shrug off crosswinds
It responds more slowly, so it needs more room to change direction
It handles much like a car once it is moving

content.explanation: A motorcycle is more responsive than a car, but it is also more sensitive to outside forces like irregular road surfaces and crosswinds.

guide.text: A motorcycle responds faster than a car but is more sensitive to rough roads and crosswinds.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles.

content.question: You can't avoid riding over a small obstacle in the road. What should you do as you reach it?

choices.text: Rise slightly off the seat and roll on a little throttle just before contact
Stay firmly in the seat and brake hard just as your front tire reaches it
Rise slightly off the seat and brake hard just as your front tire reaches it
Stay seated and pull in the clutch so the motorcycle coasts across it

content.explanation: Watch for bumps, potholes and debris, and avoid them by slowing or going around when you can. If you must ride over one, slow down as much as possible and keep the motorcycle straight. Rise slightly off the seat, weight on the footrests, so your knees and elbows absorb the shock, and roll on the throttle slightly just before contact to lighten the front end.

guide.text: To ride over an obstacle: slow down first, keep the motorcycle straight, rise slightly off the seat, and roll on a little throttle just before contact.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles.

content.question: You have just ridden over an object in the road, and the motorcycle still feels normal. What should you do?

choices.text: Get off the road and inspect the tires and rims
Keep riding, since any damage would already show in the handling
Check the tires at your next fuel stop
Ride a short way faster to test the steering

content.explanation: Once you have ridden over something, get off the road and look over both tires and both rims before going any farther, even if nothing feels wrong.

guide.text: After you ride over an obstacle, inspect the tires and rims off the road before going on.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: When is wet pavement especially slippery?

choices.text: Just after rain starts, before the oil washes to the side
After hours of steady rain have soaked the road surface
Once the rain has stopped and the road begins to dry out
Only where water has pooled deep enough to form puddles

content.explanation: Wet pavement is especially slippery just after it starts to rain, before surface oil washes to the side of the road. Painted lane markings, steel plates and metal covers are slippery when wet too.

guide.text: Wet pavement is especially slippery just after rain starts, before surface oil washes to the side of the road.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: There is a wet curve ahead. When should you slow down?

choices.text: Before you reach the curve
Once you are leaned into it, with gentle braking
Only if the tires start to slide
As you exit, once the motorcycle is upright

content.explanation: Slow down before you reach a slippery surface to lessen your chance of skidding, since your motorcycle needs more distance to stop. It matters most before a wet curve.

guide.text: Slow down before a slippery surface, and especially before a wet curve.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: On a slippery surface, what can cause a skid?

choices.text: Any sudden change in speed or direction
Hard braking, but not a sudden turn
A sudden turn, but not hard braking
Only shifting gears too quickly

content.explanation: A slippery surface leaves little traction to spare, so any abrupt change in speed or direction can start a skid. Keep your braking, steering, shifting and throttle smooth.

guide.text: On a slippery surface, keep every control smooth; an abrupt change in speed or direction can start a skid.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: You need to slow down on a wet, slippery road. How should you use the front brake?

choices.text: Use it, squeezing gradually so the wheel does not lock
Leave it alone and slow with the rear brake only
Squeeze it hard so the tire bites through the water
Pump it quickly on and off to keep the wheel turning

content.explanation: The front brake is still effective, even on a slippery surface. Use both brakes gently, squeezing the front lever gradually so the wheel does not lock.

guide.text: The front brake still works on a slippery surface. Use both brakes, squeezing the front gradually.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles.

content.question: You must ride over a small obstacle you could not avoid. At what angle should you approach it?

choices.text: As close to a right angle as you can
At a shallow angle, so the tire rolls onto it gradually
At a slant, so the front tire glances off it
Angle does not matter if you slow down first

content.explanation: Cross an obstacle you can't avoid at a right angle, or as near to one as you can manage. Keep your eyes on the line you want; where you look is how you hold your path.

guide.text: Approach an obstacle you must ride over as close to a right angle as possible.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: It has just started to rain. Where in your lane should you ride?

choices.text: In a tire track, often the left one
In the center, between the tire tracks
Near the edge, close to the shoulder
Always in the right tire track, nearest the curb

content.explanation: When rain begins, the tire tracks are the better place to ride, and the left track is often best, traffic and the road allowing. The middle of the lane is where cars drip oil, and rain turns that strip slick.

guide.text: When rain begins, ride in a tire track, often the left one, and keep off the oily center strip.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: You are coming to a stop at a busy intersection. What should you check before putting your foot down?

choices.text: That there is no oil spot where it will land
That it lands on the painted stop line, which gives the best grip
That it lands on loose grit, which keeps your boot from sliding
Nothing, as long as the motorcycle has fully stopped

content.explanation: Look at where your boot will land before you put it down at a stop or when parking. An oil spot can make it slide out from under you, and you can fall.

guide.text: Check for oil wherever your foot will land when you stop or park.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: Where do dirt and gravel tend to collect on a paved road?

choices.text: Along the sides, especially on curves and highway ramps
In the center of the lane, between the tire tracks
On bridges and overpasses
Evenly across the lane, wherever traffic is light

content.explanation: Loose dirt and gravel build up at the edges of the road, most of all on curves and on highway on- and off-ramps, so be wary of the edge in those places.

guide.text: Expect dirt and gravel at the road's edges, most of all on curves and highway ramps.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: On a cold day, where are patches of ice most likely to form?

choices.text: Low or shaded spots, and bridges and overpasses
On sunny stretches, where snow has melted first
Evenly across the road, wherever it is wet
Mostly on gravel roads rather than paved ones

content.explanation: Snow melts faster on some parts of a road than on others. Patches of ice tend to form in low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses.

guide.text: Ice tends to form in low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Slippery Surfaces.

content.question: You cannot avoid a stretch of ice or snow. How should you ride across it?

choices.text: Upright and as slowly as possible, staying off the brakes
Leaned slightly, with steady pressure on the rear brake
Briskly, so you spend as little time on it as possible
In a low gear, with bursts of throttle for grip

content.explanation: Avoid roads covered with ice or snow if you can. If you can't, keep the motorcycle straight up, go as slowly as possible and keep off the brakes. At a walking pace, you can let your feet skim the surface, and squeeze the clutch to coast if possible.

guide.text: On ice or snow you can't avoid: stay upright, go as slowly as possible, and keep off the brakes.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Railroad Tracks, Trolley Tracks and Pavement Seams.

content.question: Railroad tracks cross your road at an angle. How should you usually cross them?

choices.text: Ride straight across within your lane
Turn so you cross them at a right angle
Swerve across them at the last moment
Edge across slowly, one tire at a time

content.explanation: Crossing tracks straight on, without leaving your lane, is usually the safer choice. Swinging around to meet them at a right angle can put you in another lane of traffic.

guide.text: Cross tracks straight, staying in your lane. Steering to meet them at a right angle can put you in another lane.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Railroad Tracks, Trolley Tracks and Pavement Seams.

content.question: A track or pavement seam runs alongside your path, and you need to cross it. What should you do?

choices.text: Move away, then cross at 45 degrees or more with a decisive turn
Edge across it gradually, keeping the angle as shallow as possible
Brake firmly just as your front tire meets the seam
Steer onto it and ride along it until it fades out

content.explanation: For tracks and seams that run alongside your path, move far enough away to cross them at an angle of at least 45 degrees, then make a decisive turn across. Edging across can catch your tires and throw you off balance.

guide.text: To cross a track or seam running alongside you, move away and cross at 45 degrees or more with a decisive turn.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Grooves and Gratings.

content.question: Riding over a bridge grating, you feel the motorcycle start to weave. What should you do?

choices.text: Hold your speed and go straight across
Slow down sharply until the weaving stops
Turn to cross at an angle and get off it sooner
Grip the bars tightly and steer against the weave

content.explanation: Grooved pavement and bridge gratings can set a motorcycle weaving. Hold your speed and go straight across; angling over them only makes you zigzag to stay in your lane.

guide.text: If grooves or a grating set the motorcycle weaving, hold your speed and go straight across.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Tire Failure.

content.question: How can you usually tell that a tire has gone flat, and which one?

choices.text: By the handling: heavy steering means the front, jerking or swaying means the rear
By the handling: heavy steering means the rear, jerking or swaying means the front
By the bang or hiss, which you will hear from the side that failed
You can't tell until you stop and look at the tires

content.explanation: A flat rarely makes a sound, so the handling is your warning. A front flat makes the steering heavy, which is especially dangerous because you need to steer to stay balanced. A rear flat lets the back of the motorcycle jerk or sway.

guide.text: You seldom hear a flat. A front flat makes the steering feel heavy; a rear flat makes the back jerk or sway.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Tire Failure.

content.question: A tire goes flat while you are riding. What should you do first?

choices.text: Hold the grips firmly, roll off gently and steer straight
Brake hard with both brakes to stop as quickly as you can
Pull in the clutch at once and steer for the shoulder
Speed up slightly to keep the motorcycle stable

content.explanation: With a flat, control comes first: hold the grips firmly, roll off the throttle gently and keep the motorcycle running straight. Once it has slowed, ease over to the roadside, pull in the clutch and stop.

guide.text: With a flat: grip firmly, roll off gently and steer straight, then once slowed, move to the roadside, pull in the clutch and stop.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Tire Failure.

content.question: Your rear tire has gone flat and you need to slow down. How should you brake?

choices.text: Gradually, with the front brake only
Firmly with both brakes, as in any quick stop
With the rear brake only, to spare the good tire
Hard with the front brake, since it does most of the stopping

content.explanation: Brake only with the wheel whose tire still holds air, building the pressure gradually, and only if you are certain which tire is flat. With the rear flat, that means the front brake.

guide.text: With a flat tire, brake gradually and only with the brake of the good tire, if you are sure which one is flat.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Stuck Throttle.

content.question: Your throttle sticks open, and twisting it back and forth does not free it. What should you do?

choices.text: Hit the engine cut-off switch while pulling in the clutch
Pull in the clutch and let the engine rev until the cable frees
Brake hard and keep the engine running so you still have power
Keep twisting the throttle until the cable frees itself

content.explanation: A few twists back and forth can free a stuck throttle cable. If they don't, kill the engine with the cut-off switch, pulling in the clutch as you do it. That cuts power to the rear wheel, even if the engine takes a moment to sound quieter. Get to a safe place and stop, and don't ride on until the throttle moves freely.

guide.text: If a stuck throttle won't free with a few twists, kill the engine with its cut-off switch as you pull in the clutch.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Wobble.

content.question: Without warning, your handlebars and front wheel begin shaking side to side. What is the usual cause?

choices.text: Wrong tire pressure, the load, or unsuitable accessories
A rear tire that is slowly losing its air pressure
Using the front brake on its own at low speed
Riding in too high a gear for the speed you are going

content.explanation: This is a wobble, and it can start at any speed. The usual culprits are tire pressure, the way the motorcycle is loaded, and accessories that don't suit it. Carry heavy cargo lower and farther forward, match tire pressure and suspension to the weight, and if the wobble persists, have the steering, front wheel and bearings inspected.

guide.text: A wobble, the front wheel and bars shaking side to side, usually traces to the load, accessories or tire pressure.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Wobble.

content.question: Your motorcycle starts to wobble. What should you do?

choices.text: Grip the bars firmly, don't fight it, and ease off the throttle
Accelerate out of the wobble to steady the motorcycle
Brake firmly to slow down as quickly as you can
Hold the bars loosely and let the front wheel find its line

content.explanation: Grip the handlebars firmly, but don't fight the wobble, and close the throttle gradually to slow down. Don't brake, which could make it worse, and don't try to accelerate out of it. Move your weight as far forward and down as you can, and pull off the road as soon as possible.

guide.text: In a wobble: grip firmly without fighting it, close the throttle gradually, don't brake, and pull off as soon as you can.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Drive Train Problems.

content.question: Your drive chain breaks while you are riding. What will you notice, and what should you do?

choices.text: The rear wheel loses all drive; roll off and brake to a stop
Heavy steering at the front; hold a straight line and ease off
The engine stalls at once; restart it and ride on carefully
Nothing at first; keep riding and check the chain at your next stop

content.explanation: A broken chain or belt cuts drive to the rear wheel at once, and one that slips or snaps can also lock that wheel into a skid. Ease the throttle closed and brake to a stop somewhere safe. Regular inspection and adjustment keep this rare.

guide.text: If the chain or belt breaks, the rear wheel loses drive at once. Roll off and brake to a stop somewhere safe.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Engine Seizure.

content.question: The first sign that your engine is seizing may be a loss of power or a change in its sound. What should you do?

choices.text: Squeeze the clutch, pull off the road and check the oil
Open the throttle to keep the engine turning over
Shift down a gear to bring the engine speed up
Keep riding gently until you reach a service station

content.explanation: Seizure usually means the engine has run low on oil, so its parts bind instead of moving freely. Pull in the clutch to free the rear wheel from the engine, get off the road and stop, then check the oil and let the engine cool before you restart it.

guide.text: If the engine starts to seize, squeeze the clutch, pull off and check the oil.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Animals.

content.question: You are riding in traffic when a small animal darts into your lane. What should you do?

choices.text: Stay in your lane, avoiding it only if you safely can
Swerve into the next lane to miss it
Swerve onto the shoulder to miss it
Brake as hard as you can, even with cars close behind you

content.explanation: Miss the animal if you safely can, but with traffic around you, keep to your lane. Striking a small animal is less of a threat to you than striking something large, such as a car.

guide.text: Avoid an animal if you safely can, but in traffic stay in your lane. Hitting something small beats hitting a car.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Animals.

content.question: A dog starts chasing your motorcycle. What should you do?

choices.text: Downshift, approach slowly, then speed up past it
Stop and wait until the dog loses interest
Kick out at it to keep it clear of the motorcycle
Swerve around it without changing your speed

content.explanation: Downshift and approach the animal slowly. As you reach it, accelerate and leave it behind. Don't kick at it. Keep control of your motorcycle and look where you want to go.

guide.text: Chased by a dog: downshift and approach slowly, then accelerate away. Don't kick at it.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Animals.

content.question: A deer is standing beside the road ahead. What should you do?

choices.text: Brake and prepare to stop, since you can't predict what it will do
Downshift, approach slowly, then speed up past it
Sound your horn and hold your speed
Swerve wide around it without slowing

content.explanation: Larger animals such as deer, elk and cattle are unpredictable, so you can't count on which way they will move. Brake and prepare to stop.

guide.text: For large animals such as deer, elk or cattle, brake and prepare to stop. They are unpredictable.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Flying Objects.

content.question: A pebble kicked up by the vehicle ahead hits your face shield hard. What should you do?

choices.text: Keep your eyes on the road and hands on the bars
Lift the shield right away to check it for damage
Brake hard and stop right where you are
Turn your head away in case more stones follow

content.explanation: Bugs and stones thrown up by traffic hit riders now and then, and without face protection one can strike your eye, face or mouth. Whatever hits you, keep looking at the road and keep both hands on the grips.

guide.text: If anything strikes you while riding, keep looking at the road and keep both hands on the grips.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Getting Off the Road.

content.question: You need to pull off the road to check your motorcycle. What should you do before you turn off?

choices.text: Check the ground is firm, then signal and check mirror and blind spot
Brake firmly and early so the driver behind sees your brake light
Turn off quickly so you spend less time slowing down in traffic
Wait until you are safely on the shoulder before you signal

content.explanation: Make sure the roadside is firm enough to ride on, and slow way down if it is soft grass, loose sand or you are not sure. Drivers behind might not expect you to slow, so give a clear signal, and check your mirror and make a head check before you act.

guide.text: Before pulling off the road: check the roadside is firm, signal clearly, and check your mirror and blind spot.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Getting Off the Road.

content.question: You have pulled off the road to rest. Where should you stop the motorcycle?

choices.text: Well clear of the road, on firm, level ground
Right at the edge of the pavement, where drivers can see you
Close to the pavement, so you can pull back out easily
On the sloped part of the shoulder, so rain drains away

content.explanation: Pull well clear of the road. Drivers have a hard time spotting a motorcycle parked at the roadside, and another vehicle may choose the same spot to pull off. Pick firm, level ground too, since a stand is hard to set on a loose or sloping shoulder.

guide.text: Stop well clear of the road, on firm, level ground. A parked motorcycle is hard to see, and a stand won't set well on a loose or sloping shoulder.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Carrying Passengers and Cargo.

content.question: Who should carry a passenger or a large load?

choices.text: Only experienced riders, since the weight changes the handling
Any licensed rider, since a passenger barely changes the handling
New riders, so they can get used to the extra weight early
Only riders whose motorcycle has a larger engine

content.explanation: A passenger or a heavy load alters how the motorcycle handles, so carrying either is for experienced riders, and even they should practice with the added weight first.

guide.text: Carrying a passenger or heavy load is for experienced riders; the added weight alters the handling.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Equipment for Carrying a Passenger.

content.question: What protective gear should your passenger wear?

choices.text: The same level of protective gear as you
A helmet, with lighter gear than yours elsewhere
Whatever they find comfortable for a short ride
Less than you, since you shield them from the wind

content.explanation: Make sure your passenger is properly dressed for the ride, wearing the same level of protective gear as you.

guide.text: A passenger wears the same level of protective gear as the rider.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: Where should a child passenger sit?

choices.text: Directly behind the rider
In front of the rider, where you can keep hold of them
In front of the rider, so you can see them at all times
Either place, as long as they can reach a footrest

content.explanation: Seat a child directly behind you, never in front. Up front, a child can't balance properly and can get in the way of your control.

guide.text: A child passenger sits directly behind the rider, never in front.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: Your passenger rides a motorcycle of their own. Should you still give them instructions before you set off?

choices.text: Yes, always give complete instructions before you start
No, a rider already knows what a passenger should do
Only if they have never been a passenger before
Only if the trip will include highway riding

content.explanation: Give your passenger complete instructions before you start, even if they ride a motorcycle themselves. Never assume a passenger already knows what to do.

guide.text: Always instruct your passenger before setting off, even one who rides.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: Your passenger is about to climb on. How should you have the motorcycle ready?

choices.text: Engine running in neutral, both your feet down, brake on
Engine off, with the side stand down to hold it steady
Engine running in first gear, ready to pull away
Engine running, with you still standing beside it

content.explanation: Tell your passenger to get on only after you have started the engine and shifted into neutral. As they mount, keep both your feet on the ground and the brake applied.

guide.text: A passenger gets on only after the engine is running in neutral, with both your feet down and the brake on.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: Where should your passenger sit, and what should they hold on to?

choices.text: As far forward as possible, holding your waist, hips or belt
As far back as possible, to leave you more room to steer
Wherever they like, holding on to the edges of the seat
Right up against you, gripping your arms for balance

content.explanation: Your passenger should sit as far forward as possible without crowding you or hindering your control, and hold firmly to your waist, hips or belt.

guide.text: A passenger sits as far forward as possible without crowding you, holding your waist, hips or belt.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: What should your passenger do with their feet and legs?

choices.text: Both feet on the footrests even at stops, legs clear of the muffler
Put their feet down at stops to help you hold the motorcycle up
Let their legs hang loose so they can help balance the motorcycle
Lift their feet off the footrests whenever you turn

content.explanation: Tell your passenger to keep both feet planted on the footrests the whole ride, stops included, and to keep their legs clear of the muffler, the chain and anything else that moves.

guide.text: A passenger keeps both feet on the footrests, even at stops, and legs clear of the muffler and chains.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: How should your passenger ride through a turn?

choices.text: Directly behind you, looking over your shoulder into the turn
Leaning the opposite way to help balance the motorcycle
Turned partway around, watching traffic behind you
Looking straight ahead at the middle of your back

content.explanation: Your passenger should stay squarely behind you and, in a turn, look past your shoulder toward where you are turning. That helps the two of you lean as one.

guide.text: A passenger stays directly behind you and looks over your shoulder into turns.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Passenger to Ride.

content.question: When should your passenger tighten their hold on you?

choices.text: As you near bumps, start from a stop, or make a sudden move
Only when you are braking hard for a stop
Only once you are up to highway speed
Never, since a tight hold makes it hard for you to steer

content.explanation: Tell your passenger to tighten their hold when you approach surface hazards like bumps, are about to start from a stop, or are about to turn sharply or make a sudden move. The rest of the time, they should avoid unnecessary talk and movement.

guide.text: A passenger tightens their hold for bumps, starting off, and sudden moves such as sharp turns.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Riding With Passengers.

content.question: How does a heavier passenger change the way your motorcycle responds?

choices.text: It takes longer to speed up, slow down and turn
It stops sooner, since the weight presses the tires down
It turns more quickly, since the weight helps it lean
It makes little difference once you are moving

content.explanation: A passenger changes how your motorcycle responds. The more they weigh, the longer it takes to turn, to slow and to pick up speed.

guide.text: A heavier passenger means more time to turn, slow down and gain speed.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Riding With Passengers.

content.question: You are carrying a passenger. How should you change the way you ride?

choices.text: Ride a little slower, start slowing earlier and wait for larger gaps
Ride a little faster, so the extra weight keeps you stable
Brake later and harder, since the weight helps you stop
Ride just as you would alone

content.explanation: Ride a little slower, especially through curves, corners and bumps. Start slowing earlier as you approach a stop, keep a larger space cushion, and wait for larger gaps to cross, enter or merge with traffic.

guide.text: With a passenger: ride a little slower, start slowing earlier, keep a larger cushion and wait for larger gaps.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Preparing Your Motorcycle.

content.question: You are about to carry a passenger for the first time. What should you adjust on the motorcycle?

choices.text: Both tire pressures and the suspension, for the extra weight
Only the rear tire, since that is where the weight goes
Nothing, as long as you stay within the weight limit
The handlebars, raised to give the passenger room

content.explanation: Check the air pressure in both tires against your owner's manual, not just the rear, and adjust the suspension for the added weight.

guide.text: Before carrying a passenger or heavy load, check both tire pressures and adjust the suspension for the weight.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo.

content.question: Where should you carry a heavy load on your motorcycle?

choices.text: Low, and over or in front of the rear axle
High on a rack behind the seat, out of the way
Behind the rear axle, to balance a passenger's weight
All in one saddlebag, so it is easy to reach

content.explanation: Keep the load low and over or in front of the rear axle. Mounting it high raises the center of gravity and can upset the motorcycle's balance, and a load behind the rear axle affects how it turns and brakes and can cause a wobble. If you use saddlebags, load each with about the same weight, or the motorcycle can pull to one side.

guide.text: Carry loads low and over or in front of the rear axle, with saddlebags evenly loaded.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo.

content.question: What is the best way to fasten a load to your motorcycle?

choices.text: Elastic cords with more than one attachment point per side
Rope, pulled tight and tied off with strong knots
A single strap run across the top of the load
Loosely, so the load can shift with the motorcycle

content.explanation: Fasten the load securely with elastic cords or nets, with more than one attachment point per side. Rope can stretch and knots can come loose, letting the load shift or fall, and a loose load can catch in the wheel or chain and lock it. Stop and check the load often.

guide.text: Fasten loads with elastic cords, using more than one attachment point per side, and check them often.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo.

content.question: You are mounting a tank bag. What should you make sure of?

choices.text: It is secure and clear of the controls and brake lines
It sits high enough on the tank to be easy to reach
It is packed completely full so nothing shifts inside
It is strapped loosely so it can move with the steering

content.explanation: Mount a tank bag securely so it does not block your view of the controls or instruments, packing it only partly full if needed. When strapping it in place, make sure it does not catch any brake lines or cables near the steering head.

guide.text: Mount a tank bag securely, clear of the controls, instruments and brake lines.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Pre-Ride Test.

content.question: Your motorcycle is fully loaded for a trip. What should you do before setting out?

choices.text: Take a test ride on familiar roads to get a feel for it
Head straight for the highway so the load can settle
Nothing more, once the load is strapped down
Test the brakes with a hard stop in traffic

content.explanation: Stay within the motorcycle's gross vehicle weight rating, then take a test ride through familiar roads. Check that nothing scrapes over bumps or in turns, that the tank bag doesn't restrict the steering, and that the load won't hit your back under hard braking. Expect less power, longer passing times and longer stops.

guide.text: Test-ride a fully loaded motorcycle on familiar roads before a trip. Expect weaker acceleration and longer stops.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: Before a group ride, why should every rider know the route?

choices.text: So a separated rider never has to hurry
So the group can do without a lead rider
So the riders can take turns in the lead
So the group can skip the planned rest stops

content.explanation: Hold a riders' meeting before setting out to go over the route, how long each stretch is, rest stops, and where to stop for fuel, meals and lodging. If everyone knows the route, a rider who gets separated won't have to hurry to keep from getting lost or taking a wrong turn.

guide.text: Before a group ride, hold a riders' meeting on the route, stops and fuel, so a rider who gets separated never has to hurry.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: On a group ride, which rider sets the pace for the group?

choices.text: The last rider in the group
The lead rider, riding up front
Each rider, at their own safe speed
Whichever rider planned the route

content.explanation: The last rider sets the pace for the group. The lead and last riders should be the group's most experienced, and the leader watches ahead for changes in the road, traffic or weather and signals early, so the word gets back to everyone in time.

guide.text: The last rider sets the group's pace. The lead and last riders should be the most experienced.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: On a group ride, where should the least experienced riders ride?

choices.text: Just behind the lead rider
At the back, so no one waits on them
Leading the group, to set a pace they can handle
Side by side with an experienced rider

content.explanation: Place inexperienced riders just behind the leader. That way they never have to chase after the group, and the more experienced riders behind can watch them.

guide.text: Put inexperienced riders just behind the leader, so they never chase the group and riders behind can watch them.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: A rider in your group wants to go faster than the others. What should they do?

choices.text: Ride ahead to an agreed meeting point
Pass the other riders whenever it is safe
Ride close behind the leader to pick up the pace
Ask the whole group to speed up to match

content.explanation: A group ride is not a race. Riders don't pass one another inside the group except in an emergency, and nobody crowds or hurries the rider in front. Anyone who wants a faster pace rides on ahead and waits at a meeting point agreed beforehand.

guide.text: In a group, nobody races, passes inside the group or crowds the rider ahead. A faster rider goes on to an agreed meeting point.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: On a group ride, you see in your mirror that the rider behind you has fallen well back. What should the group do?

choices.text: Everyone slows down so the group stays together
Keep the pace, since every rider knows the route
Only the last rider drops back to stay with them
Pull over right away and wait on the shoulder

content.explanation: Use your mirrors to keep an eye on the rider behind you. If a rider falls behind, everyone slows down to keep the group together. If some riders can't keep up through curves, adjust the pace to the least experienced rider, or form two groups with different speeds.

guide.text: Watch the rider behind you in your mirrors. If anyone falls behind, the whole group slows down.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: What is one advantage of a group riding in close ranks?

choices.text: Other drivers can see the group more easily
Riders can talk to one another as they ride
Each rider can do without a space cushion
The leader can hold a faster pace for everyone

content.explanation: A close group takes up less space on the road, is easier to see and is less likely to be separated. Each rider still needs a space cushion, with time and distance to react to hazards.

guide.text: A close group uses less road, is easier to see and is harder to split up, but each rider still keeps a space cushion.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: Is it safe for two riders in a group to ride side by side in the same lane?

choices.text: No, neither rider has room to avoid a hazard
Yes, if both riders hold exactly the same speed
Yes, on a multi-lane highway in light traffic
Only when the riders need to talk to each other

content.explanation: Never ride directly alongside another rider in the same lane. Riding side by side cuts your space cushion and leaves you no room to move if you need to avoid a car or hazard.

guide.text: Never ride side by side with another rider in the same lane. Neither of you would have room to avoid a hazard.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: In a staggered group formation, where in the lane does the leader ride?

choices.text: The left side, with the second rider on the right
The right side, with the second rider on the left
The center, with the others in single file behind
Beside the second rider, so both can be seen

content.explanation: Staggering puts the leader toward the left of the lane and the next rider toward the right, behind them, and the pattern repeats down the group. No two riders are ever side by side.

guide.text: Staggered formation: the leader rides the left side of the lane, the second rider the right, and so on, alternating.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: Your group is riding in a staggered formation. When should it move into single file?

choices.text: In curves, turns, and entering or leaving a highway
Whenever the traffic around the group gets heavy
When cruising on a long, straight stretch of highway
Whenever one of the riders falls behind the group

content.explanation: Move into single file when riding in curves, turning, and entering or leaving a highway.

guide.text: Ride single file in curves, in turns, and entering or leaving a highway.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: Your group is riding in a staggered formation and needs to pass a slower car, using the oncoming lane. How should it pass?

choices.text: One rider at a time, each when it is safe
All together, close behind the leader
Two at a time, to cut time in the oncoming lane
The leader first, then everyone else at once

content.explanation: When the pass takes you into the oncoming lane, riders in a staggered formation pass one at a time. The leader pulls out and passes first when it is safe, then the second rider moves up to the left side of the lane to make their own pass, and the rest follow the same way.

guide.text: Passing through the oncoming lane, a staggered group goes one rider at a time, the leader first, each from the left side of the lane.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Group Riding.

content.question: Your group is passing a slower car one rider at a time. After the leader passes, where in the lane should the leader ride?

choices.text: The left side, holding passing speed
The right side, to make room for the next rider
The center, slowing so the others catch up
Whichever side has the better view ahead

content.explanation: After passing, the leader returns to the left side of the lane, the lead position, and keeps riding at passing speed to open up room for the next rider. Each rider goes back to the same place in the formation they held before the pass.

guide.text: After passing, the leader returns to the left side of the lane and holds passing speed, opening room for the next rider.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Alcohol and Drugs in Motorcycle Operation.

content.question: You have had one drink and are well under the legal limit. Can it affect your riding?

choices.text: Yes, even one drink can affect it
No, not until you reach the legal limit
Not if you are used to drinking
Only if you start to feel its effects

content.explanation: A single drink is enough to change how you ride. Judgment and skill start to slip long before you reach the legal limit, and alcohol dulls your thinking along with your physical control.

guide.text: Even one drink can affect your riding. Impairment begins well below the legal limit.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Alcohol and Drugs in Motorcycle Operation.

content.question: You took an over-the-counter cold medicine this morning. What should you know before riding?

choices.text: Its side effects could make riding riskier
Over-the-counter drugs don't affect riding
It is safe as long as you haven't been drinking
It is fine if you ride slowly and carefully

content.explanation: Over-the-counter medicine, prescriptions and illegal drugs can all have side effects that raise your risk on a motorcycle. Add alcohol and the danger grows, because the two together do more harm than either one.

guide.text: Over-the-counter and prescription drugs can have side effects that make riding riskier, and with alcohol they are more dangerous still.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Blood Alcohol Concentration.

content.question: Which of these all play a major part in your blood alcohol concentration?

choices.text: How much you drink, how fast, and your body weight
The time of day, the weather, and your mood
Your age, your height, and how long you have ridden
The brand, the price, and how cold it is

content.explanation: Your blood alcohol concentration, or BAC, is the amount of alcohol in your blood. How much you drink, how fast you drink it and your body weight all play a major part. The faster you drink, the more alcohol builds up in your body.

guide.text: BAC is the amount of alcohol in your blood. How much you drink, how fast, and your body weight all play a major part.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Blood Alcohol Concentration.

content.question: Which holds the most alcohol: a 12-ounce beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine or a shot of liquor?

choices.text: None; they hold about the same
The shot, since liquor is the strongest
The beer, since it is the largest
The wine, since it is stronger than beer

content.explanation: A 12-ounce beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine and a shot of liquor each hold about the same amount of alcohol, so each counts as one drink.

guide.text: A 12-ounce beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine and a shot of liquor each hold about the same alcohol: one drink.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Blood Alcohol Concentration.

content.question: About how quickly does your body process alcohol?

choices.text: About one drink an hour
About two drinks an hour
About three drinks an hour
Faster with coffee or a cold shower

content.explanation: Your body processes alcohol at about one drink an hour. Drink faster than that and the alcohol builds up, raising your BAC.

guide.text: Your body processes alcohol at about one drink an hour. Drink faster and it builds up.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Minimize the Risks.

content.question: Which ability does alcohol affect first?

choices.text: Judging how well you are riding
Seeing clearly, as your vision blurs
Keeping your balance at low speeds
Hearing horns and sirens around you

content.explanation: Alcohol reaches your judgment of your own riding before anything else. Your riding gets steadily poorer while it feels like it is improving, and that false confidence draws you into bigger risks.

guide.text: Alcohol dulls your judgment of your own riding first, so you feel more capable as you get worse and take bigger risks.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Make an Intelligent Choice.

content.question: You'll be riding home later. Why is setting yourself a drink limit a poor plan?

choices.text: Once you start, your resistance weakens
A limit is only a problem for new riders
It isn't; a limit keeps you under the legal BAC
It isn't, as long as you pace your drinks

content.explanation: Once you start drinking, your resistance gets weaker and your judgment is affected. The safest choice is not to drink if you will be riding, and not to ride if you have been drinking.

guide.text: If you'll be riding, don't drink: once you start, your resistance weakens. If you have been drinking, don't ride.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Make an Intelligent Choice.

content.question: Before riding, you waited an hour for each drink you had. Which is true?

choices.text: Side effects from the drinking may still remain
Your riding skills will no longer be affected
You are certain to be back under the legal limit
You will be fine as long as you ride slowly

content.explanation: An hour per drink is only a rough guide, since many factors affect how much alcohol your body holds on to, and its fatiguing after-effects can outlast it. If you have been drinking, wait until your system has eliminated both.

guide.text: Waiting an hour per drink doesn't guarantee you're fit to ride. Side effects can remain.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Step In to Protect a Friend.

content.question: A friend has had too much to drink and is about to ride home. What should you do?

choices.text: Step in and keep them from riding
Let them decide, since it is their choice
Follow them home to make sure they are safe
Tell them to ride slowly and carefully

content.explanation: Someone who has had too much to drink can't make a responsible decision, so it is up to others to step in. Arrange a safe ride home, slow the pace of their drinking, keep them from getting on the motorcycle, take their key if you can, and get other friends to help.

guide.text: A friend who has had too much to drink can't decide responsibly. Step in: arrange a ride, keep them there, take their key.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Cannabis & Motorcycle Operation.

content.question: Even where cannabis is legal, why is it unsafe to ride after using it?

choices.text: It distorts your sense of time, space and speed
It is only unsafe when combined with alcohol
It is only unsafe if it was eaten, not smoked
Its effects wear off within a few minutes

content.explanation: Even where cannabis is legal, it isn't legal, safe or wise to ride while impaired by it, because it distorts your perception of time, space and speed. Smoked, its effects can begin within minutes and last 2 to 4 hours; eaten, they may take over an hour to start and last more than 6 hours.

guide.text: Even where cannabis is legal, don't ride impaired by it. It distorts your sense of time, space and speed.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Fatigue.

content.question: Compared with driving a car, how quickly does riding a motorcycle tire you out?

choices.text: Faster, so you'll tire sooner on a long trip
About the same, over a trip of the same length
More slowly, since you're out in the fresh air
More slowly, as long as you are dressed warmly

content.explanation: Riding a motorcycle is more tiring than driving a car, so on a long trip you'll tire sooner. Wind, cold and rain tire you quickly too: dress warmly, and a windshield is worth its cost on long rides.

guide.text: Riding tires you faster than driving a car. Wind, cold and rain tire you quickly, so dress warmly.

meta.sourceSection: Being in Shape to Ride, under Fatigue.

content.question: On a long ride, what is the best way to fight fatigue?

choices.text: Get off and rest at least every two hours
Take a stimulant once you begin to feel tired
Push on so the ride ends sooner
Open your visor for some fresh air

content.explanation: Fatigue can affect your control of the motorcycle. Take frequent rest breaks, stopping and getting off the motorcycle at least every two hours. Artificial stimulants are no answer: they often bring extreme fatigue or depression as they wear off.

guide.text: Fatigue costs you control. Stop and get off the motorcycle at least every two hours, and don't rely on stimulants.

meta.sourceSection: Wear the Right Gear, under Clothing.

content.question: It is cold and wet out. Why does it matter that your clothes keep you warm and dry?

choices.text: Getting cold makes the bike harder to control
It only matters for comfort, not for control
Being chilled keeps you more alert
Cold mainly affects the engine, not the rider

content.explanation: In cold or wet weather, dress to stay warm and dry, with a jacket that keeps out the wind. Getting cold makes it harder to control the motorcycle, and long rides in the cold can chill you badly.

guide.text: Dress warm and dry in cold or wet weather. Getting cold makes the motorcycle harder to control.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, under Get Familiar with the Controls.

content.question: You are about to ride a motorcycle you have never ridden before. Besides finding its controls, what should you do?

choices.text: Work its controls first, then ride very cautiously
Ride it as you would your own, once it is checked
Trust your experience, since all controls work alike
Leave extra stopping room only if it is heavier

content.explanation: Before moving off, work the brakes, clutch, throttle and shifter a few times. Once underway, ride with extra care: go easy on the throttle, slow down more for turns and give yourself more room to stop.

guide.text: On an unfamiliar motorcycle, work the controls a few times first, then ride cautiously: gentle throttle, slower turns, extra stopping room.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, under Check Your Motorcycle.

content.question: How often should you check your motorcycle before riding it?

choices.text: Before every ride
Before long trips only
Every few hundred miles
Only when something feels wrong

content.explanation: Check your motorcycle before every ride, not just before long trips. Read its owner's manual, and keep the motorcycle in good condition between rides.

guide.text: Check your motorcycle before every ride. Read the owner's manual and keep the motorcycle in good condition.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, Check Your Motorcycle, under Tires and Wheels.

content.question: In a pre-ride check, you try each brake lever one at a time. What should you find?

choices.text: Each feels firm and holds the motorcycle by itself
Each moves all the way to the grip without effort
Only the front needs to hold the motorcycle
A little sponginess, which is normal

content.explanation: Try the front and rear brakes one at a time. Each should feel firm and hold the motorcycle when fully applied. Try both brakes, too, to make sure each one turns on the brake light.

guide.text: Pre-ride: try each brake on its own. Each should feel firm, hold the motorcycle, and turn on the brake light.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, Check Your Motorcycle, under Controls.

content.question: In a pre-ride check, what should the throttle do when you release it?

choices.text: Snap back to fully closed
Stay where you left it until you close it
Return slowly, so the engine doesn't jerk
Hold a little open to keep the engine running

content.explanation: Try both controls before riding off. Let go of the throttle and it should spring all the way shut by itself, and the clutch should work smoothly with a tight feel.

guide.text: Before you ride, check that the throttle springs fully closed when released and that the clutch feels tight and smooth.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, Check Your Motorcycle, under Lights and Electrics.

content.question: When should you adjust your motorcycle's mirrors?

choices.text: Before you start riding
At your first stop along the way
While rolling slowly through a parking lot
Once you are up to speed, to see real traffic

content.explanation: Clean and set your mirrors before you ride off; adjusting one on the move means riding one-handed. Aim each to show the lane behind you and the lane beside you. Your arm or shoulder at the edge of the glass is fine, as long as the road behind and alongside is in view.

guide.text: Adjust your mirrors before you start riding, to show the lane behind and beside you. Seeing the edge of your arm is fine.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, Check Your Motorcycle, under Oil and Other Fluids.

content.question: How often should you check your brake hydraulic fluid and coolant, if your motorcycle has them?

choices.text: At least once a week
Only at each oil change
Once a year, at a service
Only when a warning light comes on

content.explanation: Engine oil and transmission fluid get checked before each ride; brake hydraulic fluid and coolant, at least weekly. Glance under the motorcycle for any oil or fuel leaking out.

guide.text: Check oil and transmission fluid before riding, and brake fluid and coolant weekly. Look underneath for leaks.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, Check Your Motorcycle, under Oil and Other Fluids.

content.question: Your motorcycle has a fuel valve. Why check that it is open before starting out?

choices.text: It may start on the fuel in the lines, then stall
The engine won't turn over at all with it closed
An open valve keeps fuel from leaking
It only matters on a cold morning

content.explanation: If the fuel valve is closed, the engine can still start and run on what is left in the fuel lines, then stall when that is used up. On a motorcycle with a valve, open it before you set off.

guide.text: If your motorcycle has a fuel valve, open it before starting out. Closed, the bike may start, then stall once the lines empty.

meta.sourceSection: Know Your Motorcycle, Check Your Motorcycle, under Stands.

content.question: In a pre-ride check, what should you make sure of with the side stand?

choices.text: Its spring holds it tightly in the up position
It hangs loosely, ready to drop when you stop
It stays down until the engine has warmed up
It only needs checking if it has been bent

content.explanation: Make sure the side stand operates smoothly and that its spring holds it tightly in the up position. A center stand, if your motorcycle has one, should be held firmly against the frame whenever you are moving.

guide.text: Pre-ride: the side stand's spring should hold it tightly up, and a center stand firmly against the frame.

meta.sourceSection: Pre-Ride Inspection Checklist, under Tires and Wheels.

content.question: When should you check your motorcycle's tire pressure?

choices.text: When the tires are cold
Right after a ride, while they are warm
Only when a tire looks low
Only before long trips

content.explanation: Check tire pressure when the tires are cold, and adjust it to the load you will carry.

guide.text: Check tire pressure cold, and adjust it to the load.

meta.sourceSection: Pre-Ride Inspection Checklist, under Controls.

content.question: With the engine idling, you turn the handlebars from side to side. What should the engine do?

choices.text: Keep idling steadily, without revving
Rev up slightly, which is normal
Drop its idle, then recover on its own
Rev a little, as long as the throttle snaps closed

content.explanation: The throttle should move freely and snap closed, and turning the handlebars should not make the engine rev. Cables should be routed so nothing pulls or catches at the steering head.

guide.text: Pre-ride: turning the handlebars should not rev the engine, and the throttle should snap closed.

meta.sourceSection: Pre-Ride Inspection Checklist, under Oil.

content.question: Which fluid should you check only when the engine is cool?

choices.text: Coolant
Engine oil
Brake fluid
Fuel

content.explanation: Check the coolant only when the engine is cool. Engine oil is the opposite: check it warm, with the motorcycle on its center stand on level ground.

guide.text: Check coolant only when cool. Check engine oil warm, on the center stand, on level ground.

meta.sourceSection: Pre-Ride Inspection Checklist, under Chassis.

content.question: Where along the drive chain should you check its tension?

choices.text: At its tightest point
At its loosest point
Right next to the rear sprocket
Anywhere, since it is the same all along

content.explanation: Check chain tension at its tightest point, and lubricate the chain's side plates while it is hot. Never lubricate a belt. The sprocket teeth should not be hooked.

guide.text: Check chain tension at its tightest point and lubricate the chain hot. Never lubricate a belt.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, Crash Avoidance, under Quick Stops and Front-Wheel Skids.
meta.note: The manuals say to reapply firmly, smoothly, with less pressure, or with controlled gradual pressure. Firm but smooth, short of another lock, holds for every one of them.

content.question: Your front wheel locks in a hard stop, and you let go of the brake to get it rolling. How should you put the front brake back on?

choices.text: Firmly, but squeezed on smoothly so it does not lock again
With one quick, hard grab to win back the distance you lost
Barely at all, finishing the stop mostly on the rear brake
Not until the motorcycle is almost stopped, so it cannot lock twice

content.explanation: You still need the front brake to stop, so reapply it firmly, but squeeze it on smoothly. Grabbing at the front brake is what locks the wheel.

guide.text: After a front-wheel lock, reapply the front brake firmly but smoothly, never with a grab.
